title: Robust Adaptation in E. coli Chemotaxis
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter closes out two lectures (L7–L8) on the chemotaxis pathway of *E. coli*, and answers the modelling question L8 left open: why doesn't the full biochemical model of the pathway — every receptor complex tracked by its methylation level, ligand-binding state and phosphorylation state — reproduce the *perfect adaptation* that is observed experimentally? The answer is a chain of four successive, individually-justified simplifications, each checked against an experimental fact, that collapses the full model down to a two-state module whose adaptation is not merely perfect but **robust**: exact for any attractant concentration, with no fine-tuning of rate constants required. The chapter ends where the lecture turns to the next topic, biological oscillators: it revives the one-variable fixed-point/stability recipe from problem set 1 on the autocatalytic reaction, and recasts the reduced chemotaxis network as a two-variable linear system, which is the example the next lecture uses to introduce nullclines. It assumes the chemotaxis signalling proteins from L7 — the methyl-accepting chemoreceptor Tar, the kinase CheA, the adaptor CheW, the response regulator CheY, the methylesterase CheB and the methyltransferase CheR — and the full combinatorial model built in L8, which is sketched but not re-derived here. ## The pathway, in outline *E. coli* swims by alternating **runs** (smooth, counterclockwise flagellar rotation) with **tumbles** (a randomising, clockwise burst) that reorient it. Without any attractant, the two alternate at a fixed average rate and the cell performs an unbiased random walk. With an attractant present, tumbling is suppressed for as long as the concentration the cell has recently experienced is *increasing* — the cell compares now against a few seconds ago, not one side of its body against the other, because it is far too small to sense a spatial gradient directly. This is the sense in which the slides describe the gradient as "sensed in a temporal manner": runs up the gradient are lengthened, runs down it are not, and the net effect over many run-tumble cycles is drift toward higher concentration. The sensor is a cluster of receptor complexes — Tar in complex with CheA and CheW — embedded in the membrane. Ligand (attractant) binding shifts CheA's autophosphorylation rate. The phosphate then relays: CheA-P hands it to CheY, and separately to CheB ($Y\rightleftharpoons Y_p$, $B\rightleftharpoons B_p$). CheY-P diffuses to the flagellar motor and raises the probability of clockwise rotation (tumbling); CheZ removes the phosphate again. CheB-P is the active demethylase, stripping methyl groups from the receptor; CheR, which is constitutively active, adds them back. The receptor's methylation level in turn sets its baseline kinase activity — this is the slow feedback loop that produces adaptation, and it is exactly what the reduction below is about. (Notation: $LT_{np}$ is a ligand-bound receptor complex at methylation level $n$, phosphorylated; $LT_{np}\to LT_n$ is the loss of that phosphate, feeding the $Y/B$ cycles.) The full model (following Spiro, Parkinson and Othmer's 1997 model of excitation and adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis$^{[1]}$) tracks every combination of these three degrees of freedom — methylation level ($T_2,T_3,T_4,\dots$), ligand occupancy ($T_n$ vs $LT_n$) and phosphorylation ($T_n$ vs $T_{np}$) — as a lattice of states connected by reversible reactions along three axes. It is this lattice, not any one piece of it, that must be shown to reproduce perfect adaptation; and it does not, without extra assumptions. ## Perfect adaptation, and why the full model doesn't guarantee it **Perfect adaptation** is the experimental observation that after a step change in attractant concentration, the pathway's output — the phosphorylation level driving CheY-P, and so the tumbling bias — relaxes back exactly to its pre-stimulus value, however large the step. A model that reproduces this only for some settings of its rate constants, or only over part of the ligand range, is not the phenomenon: real cells adapt this way robustly, without having their internal rate constants tuned by hand. The question the lecture works through is which of the simplifications one can make to the full lattice model turn perfect adaptation from an occasional fine-tuned accident into a structural guarantee. ## First reduction: lumping methylation states The first simplification lumps the methylation ladder into two effective classes, "2" and "3", each of which can be unphosphorylated or phosphorylated, and unliganded or liganded: $$\begin{matrix} \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_{2p}\\ \text{LT}_{2p}\end{bmatrix} & \xrightarrow{k_{eff4}(L)} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_{3p}\\ \text{LT}_{3p}\end{bmatrix}\\ & \xleftarrow{k_{eff3}(L)} & \\ k_{eff1}(L)\Big\uparrow\Big\downarrow k_{pt} & & k_{eff2}(L)\Big\uparrow\Big\downarrow k_{pt}\\ \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_2\\ \text{LT}_2\end{bmatrix} & \xrightarrow{k_{eff4}(L)} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_3\\ \text{LT}_3\end{bmatrix}\\ & \xleftarrow{k_{eff3}(L)} & \end{matrix}$$ Horizontally, methylation and demethylation move a complex between class 2 and class 3 at ligand-dependent effective rates $k_{eff3}(L)$, $k_{eff4}(L)$. Vertically, phosphorylation is ligand-dependent and methylation-class-dependent ($k_{eff1}(L)$ for class 2, $k_{eff2}(L)$ for class 3), while dephosphorylation — phosphotransfer onward to CheY and CheB — runs at a single rate $k_{pt}$ that does not depend on ligand at all. Phosphorylation/dephosphorylation is fast enough, relative to the slow methylation reaction, that it can be treated as pre-equilibrated for whichever methylation class a receptor currently sits in. What is then slow, and carries the memory of past stimulation, is the *methylation-class balance* itself: $$\alpha \equiv \frac{[3]}{[2]+[3]}$$ and the net phosphorylation rate is the class-weighted average of the two class-specific rates, $$k_{phos} = (1-\alpha)\,k_{eff1}(L) + \alpha\,k_{eff2}(L).$$ Because $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $k_{phos}$ is, for each fixed $L$, pinned between $k_{eff1}(L)$ and $k_{eff2}(L)$: it cannot leave that band no matter how $\alpha$ is chosen. Perfect adaptation asks for something stronger than "pinned at each $L$" — it asks for a *single, $L$-independent* target rate that some choice of $\alpha(L)$ can hold across the *whole* range of $L$. That is only possible if the two bounding curves overlap consistently as $L$ varies: the target must lie above every value $k_{eff1}(L)$ ever reaches, and below every value $k_{eff2}(L)$ ever falls to. That is the problem with stopping the reduction here: perfect adaptation is achievable, but only for parameter choices that happen to leave a "safe zone" between the two curves across the full range of $L$ — a fine-tuning condition, not a structural guarantee. Two more assumptions are needed to remove the fine-tuning altogether. ## Second and third reductions: where CheB acts, and why methylation saturates **Second reduction.** Add the assumption that **CheB only demethylates phosphorylated receptors** — the backward (demethylating) reaction on the unphosphorylated row disappears: $$\begin{matrix} \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_{2p}\\ \text{LT}_{2p}\end{bmatrix} & \xrightarrow{k_{eff3}(L)} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_{3p}\\ \text{LT}_{3p}\end{bmatrix}\\ & \xleftarrow{k_{eff4}(L)} & \\ k_{eff1}(L)\Big\uparrow\Big\downarrow k_{pt} & & k_{eff2}(L)\Big\uparrow\Big\downarrow k_{pt}\\ \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_2\\ \text{LT}_2\end{bmatrix} & \xrightarrow{k_{eff3}(L)} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_3\\ \text{LT}_3\end{bmatrix} \end{matrix}$$ There is no direct experimental measurement of whether CheB acts only on active (phosphorylated) receptors. The indirect evidence offered is that the methylation rate drops immediately after ligand addition — consistent with CheB's activity tracking the receptor's activation state rather than methylation alone. **Third reduction.** Add the assumption that **CheR is saturated**: $[\text{CheR}] \ll [\text{receptors}]$, so methylation runs at a fixed, receptor-concentration-independent flux $r_{in}$ rather than a rate proportional to how many receptors sit in class 2. This removes class 2 as an explicit variable — it collapses into a constant inflow feeding class 3 directly: $$\begin{matrix} \xrightarrow{r_{in}} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_{3p}\\ \text{LT}_{3p}\end{bmatrix}\\ \xleftarrow{k_{eff4}(L)} & \\ & k_{eff2}(L)\Big\uparrow\Big\downarrow k_{pt}\\ \xrightarrow{r_{in}} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_3\\ \text{LT}_3\end{bmatrix} \end{matrix}$$ The check here is a real measurement: CheR's Michaelis constant for receptor binding is much smaller than the receptor concentration, so essentially every receptor is CheR-bound and the reaction sits at $V_{max}$ regardless of substrate level — the saturation assumption holds. ## Fourth reduction: a robust, ligand-independent output The last assumption is that **demethylation does not distinguish ligand-bound from ligand-free receptors**, so the demethylation rate $k_{eff4}$ stops depending on $L$ at all. Checked against kinetic measurements of demethylation, this holds: demethylation is nearly independent of both methylation level and ligand occupancy. The reduced network is now $$\begin{matrix} \xrightarrow{r_{in}} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_{3p}\\ \text{LT}_{3p}\end{bmatrix} & \mathbf{C^*}\\ \xleftarrow{k_{eff4}} & \\ & k_{eff2}(L)\Big\uparrow\Big\downarrow k_{pt}\\ \xrightarrow{r_{in}} & \begin{bmatrix}\text{T}_3\\ \text{LT}_3\end{bmatrix} & \mathbf{C} \end{matrix}$$ and it obeys perfect adaptation **for any value of $L$** — not just within some fine-tuned window. Writing $C^*$ for the phosphorylated pool and $C$ for the unphosphorylated one, $$\dot C^* = (-k_{pt}-k_{eff4})\,C^* + k_{eff2}(L)\,C + r_{in}, \qquad \dot C = k_{pt}\,C^* - k_{eff2}(L)\,C + r_{in}.$$ Adding the two equations, every ligand-dependent term cancels: $$\dot C^* + \dot C = -k_{eff4}\,C^* + 2r_{in}.$$ At steady state the left side vanishes, so $$[3_p] = C^*_{ss} = \frac{2\,r_{in}}{k_{eff4}}.$$ Neither $r_{in}$ (saturated CheR flux) nor $k_{eff4}$ (ligand-independent demethylation) depends on $L$ — so the steady-state phosphorylated fraction does not depend on $L$ either, for *any* $L$. This is the structural version of perfect adaptation the first reduction could only get by fine-tuning: it now follows from the shape of the network, because the only two rates that survive at steady state are the ones the last two assumptions made ligand-independent. ## Toward oscillators: fixed points and stability, revisited The lecture pivots here to the next topic — biological oscillators (the cell division cycle, circadian rhythms) — with two motivating questions: what does a reaction network need in order to oscillate, and how is that different from the switches and the chemotaxis network already covered? Answering this needs a graphical way to read differential equations, which the lecture builds up by returning to the simplest possible example: the autocatalytic reaction from problem set 1, $$A + X \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_{+1}}{\rightleftharpoons}} 2X, \qquad \dot x = k_1 a x - k_{-1}x^2, \qquad a=[A]\ \text{held constant (large excess)}.$$ This is a first-order equation of the form $\dot x = f(x)$, and the general recipe for reading one is: 1. find the fixed points, $f(x^*)=0$; 2. determine the stability of each. Here $f(x)=k_1ax-k_{-1}x^2$ is a downward parabola with two roots, $$x_1^*=0, \qquad x_2^*=\frac{k_1a}{k_{-1}},$$ and between them $f(x)>0$ (so $\dot x>0$: $x$ increases toward $x_2^*$), while beyond $x_2^*$, $f(x)<0$ (so $\dot x<0$: $x$ decreases back toward $x_2^*$). Sketching $[X]$ against time for several starting values makes the picture concrete: trajectories starting below $x_2^*$ rise toward it, trajectories starting above it fall toward it, and only a trajectory starting exactly at $x_1^*=0$ stays there. The quantitative version of "stability" perturbs around a fixed point, $\eta(t)=x(t)-x^*$, and Taylor-expands: $$f(x^*+\eta) = f(x^*) + \eta f'(x^*) + O(\eta^2) \approx \eta f'(x^*) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dot\eta \approx \eta f'(x^*) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \eta(t)\sim e^{f'(x^*)t}.$$ So $f'(x^*)>0$ means small perturbations grow — an **unstable** fixed point — and $f'(x^*)<0$ means they decay — a **stable** one. For the autocatalytic reaction, $f'(x)=k_1a-2k_{-1}x$, so $f'(x_1^*)=k_1a>0$ (unstable) and $f'(x_2^*)=k_1a-2k_1a=-k_1a<0$ (stable) — matching the picture from the phase-line argument above. ## The chemotaxis network as a linear system The lecture closes by pointing the same machinery at the reduced chemotaxis module itself, as a preview of what the next lecture (on nullclines) will need: a system in *two* variables rather than one. Writing $x\equiv C^*$, $y\equiv C$, the fourth-reduction equations above are exactly of the generic linear form $$\dot x = ax+by+r_{in}, \qquad \dot y = cx+dy+r_{in},$$ with $a\equiv-(k_{pt}+k_{eff4})$, $b\equiv k_{eff2}(L)$, $c\equiv k_{pt}$, $d\equiv -b$. A single fixed point and a single derivative no longer suffice to read off stability for a system like this — which is exactly the gap the next lecture's nullcline method is introduced to fill. ## Sources - Slides: `lectures/09-notes/01-wrapping-up-e-coli-chemotaxis-l7-l8.md` and `02-fourth-reduction.md` (MIT OCW 8.591J, Fall 2004) — the full "wrapping up" sequence: pathway background, the four reductions, the transition to oscillators, the autocatalysis recipe, and the chemotaxis network recast as a linear system. This markdown is a model's reconstruction of a PDF with no text layer; the extracted figures (`figures/p002-1.jpeg` through `p020-1.jpeg`) were checked directly against the prose to confirm the shapes of the "safe zone" plots and the autocatalysis parabola used in the figures above. - Named in the slides but not reproduced here (images removed for copyright, or simply referenced): Mittal, Budrene, Brenner and Van Oudenaarden, "Motility of *Escherichia coli* cells in clusters formed by chemotactic aggregation," *PNAS* 100(23), 2003; Spiro, Parkinson and Othmer, "A model of excitation and adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis," *PNAS* 94(14), 1997 — the source of the full reaction-lattice model this chapter reduces. - No transcript or written notes were supplied for this lecture. - The exercise set attached to this lecture slot (`psets/09-questions/*`, 8.591J Fall 2014) covers the quasispecies equation, adaptation on a sharply peaked fitness landscape, the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, stochastic simulation of the error threshold, and conditioned vs. direct response — an evolutionary-dynamics and game-theory unit from a different point in the course, not the chemotaxis/oscillator material in these slides. No exercises are reproduced here for that reason.
